He writes his drama of Prometheus’ (i 226). S. worked quickly at first, and had probably been
writing since at least his own arrival at ‘I Cappuccini’ at the end of August, for his letter of
Tuesday 22 September, written to Mary at Este from Padua, asks her to ‘bring . . . the sheets
of “Prometheus Unbound” which you will find numbered from 1 to 26 on the table of the
pavilion’ (L ii 39–40). S.’s composition on loose sheets, rather than in a notebook, explains the
almost total disappearance of draft materials for Act I; and the mention of numbered sheets
suggests that Act I may already have been in a relatively advanced state (26 sheets might imply
somewhere between 500 and 600 lines). On 8 October, S. states in a letter to Peacock that he
